variants.name: Boost.Asio completion token (bound handler)
variants.idiom_name: Boost.Asio initiating functions with a bound completion handler
variants.implementation_notes: Boost.Asio is built around this pattern: every initiating function takes a completion token as its final argument, and the library invokes exactly that token with the result, so binding the per-request state into the handler (lambda capture, std::bind, bind_executor) is the ACT and the io_context is the demultiplexer. The hand-written token table of the classic form is unnecessary in-process; what the pattern still contributes is the discipline of putting completion state where the completion arrives (owning handles, strands) instead of looking requests up again. Custom completion tokens (async_compose) and std::bind_front cover the cases where the token must be delivered elsewhere, e.g. into a queue.
pitfalls: A blocking call inside a completion handler stalls the io_context and every other outstanding operation whose token is waiting to be dispatched.
Capture owning handles (shared_ptr) rather than references: the operation outlives the enclosing scope and a dangling capture is the C++ form of a stale token.
Handlers may run concurrently when the io_context has several threads; a shared completion registry then needs its own synchronisation or a strand.

variants.name: Boost.Asio with C++20 coroutines (use_awaitable)
variants.implementation_notes: With awaitable/use_awaitable/co_spawn the compiler-generated coroutine frame holds the per-request state and each co_await registers the continuation that must run on completion, so the token becomes implicit and the callback pyramid disappears. The choice is between explicitness and linear code: keep bound-handler tokens where completions must fan out to non-coroutine consumers (queues, C APIs, plain callbacks), use coroutines where the flow is a sequence of awaits.
pitfalls: Detached co_spawn coroutines must own their state; a coroutine that refers to a connection object already destroyed is the coroutine-era successor of the dangling completion token.
Error handling changes shape: without as_tuple/redirect_error a failed operation throws, so error paths that the callback form expressed as error_code must be caught.
Cancellation has to be propagated explicitly (cancellation slots/stop tokens); a coroutine suspended on a stream that never completes occupies its frame indefinitely.
